title: What are GC roots (stack refs, static fields, JNI refs, thread objects, class loaders, monitors), how does tracing determine garbage, and why are circular references NOT a leak in Java?
shortTitle: What are GC roots and how does tracing work?

s1_definition.profdef: Garbage-collection roots are the set of references that are inherently reachable, meaning the starting points from which the collector begins tracing. They include local variables and parameters on each thread's stack, static fields of loaded classes, Java Native Interface references held by native code, live thread objects, class loaders and the classes they load, and objects used as synchronization monitors. A tracing garbage collector marks every object reachable by following references from these roots, and any object not marked is unreachable and therefore garbage. Circular references, where two objects reference each other, are not a leak in Java precisely because the collector uses reachability from roots rather than reference counting, so a cycle that no root can reach is still correctly identified as garbage.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the garbage-collection roots as the official entry points to National Bank of India's records, like the live ledgers on each teller's desk, the master registers bolted to the wall (static fields), and the records held by security staff outside the building (native references). To find which folders are still needed, an auditor starts only from these official entry points and follows every cross-reference folder-to-folder, marking each one they can reach. Any folder nobody can reach from an official entry point is scrap, even if two scrap folders happen to reference each other. Two abandoned folders stapled together in a forgotten corner are still scrap, because no official entry point leads to either of them, which is why mutual references do not save them.
s1_definition.oneliner: GC roots are the inherently reachable starting points like stack locals, static fields, and native references; the collector marks everything reachable from them and treats the rest as garbage, so a reference cycle unreachable from any root is still collected and is not a leak.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Garbage-collection roots are the set of references that are inherently reachable, meaning the starting points from which the collector begins tracing. They include local variables and parameters on each thread's stack, static fields of loaded classes, Java Native Interface references held by native code, live thread objects, class loaders and the classes they load, and objects used as synchronization monitors. A tracing garbage collector marks every object reachable by following references from these roots, and any object not marked is unreachable and therefore garbage. Circular references, where two objects reference each other, are not a leak in Java precisely because the collector uses reachability from roots rather than reference counting, so a cycle that no root can reach is still correctly identified as garbage.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the garbage-collection roots as the official entry points to National Bank of India's records, like the live ledgers on each teller's desk, the master registers bolted to the wall (static fields), and the records held by security staff outside the building (native references). To find which folders are still needed, an auditor starts only from these official entry points and follows every cross-reference folder-to-folder, marking each one they can reach. Any folder nobody can reach from an official entry point is scrap, even if two scrap folders happen to reference each other. Two abandoned folders stapled together in a forgotten corner are still scrap, because no official entry point leads to either of them, which is why mutual references do not save them.

**One line to remember:** GC roots are the inherently reachable starting points like stack locals, static fields, and native references; the collector marks everything reachable from them and treats the rest as garbage, so a reference cycle unreachable from any root is still collected and is not a leak.

sections.s2_technical:
A tracing collector decides what is garbage by reachability, and reachability is defined relative to a fixed set of roots. The roots are references that exist outside the normal object graph and are known to be live by definition. The main categories are: local variables and operand-stack entries in the frames of every running thread, because anything a currently executing method is using must be kept; static fields of loaded classes, because class statics live as long as the class is loaded; Java Native Interface references, both local and global, that native code holds so that objects passed to native code are not collected out from under it; live thread objects themselves, since a running thread is obviously alive; class loaders and the class objects they have loaded, because unloading them has its own rules; and objects currently used as monitors, meaning objects a thread is synchronizing on. There are a few others, like references held by the JVM internally, but these are the ones worth naming in an interview.

Tracing proceeds in two conceptual phases, mark and sweep. In the mark phase the collector starts from every root and performs a traversal of the object graph, following each reference to the objects it points to, then their references, and so on, marking every object it reaches as live. Because it follows references transitively, it reaches the entire set of objects that are still usable by the program. In the sweep phase, any object that was not marked is by definition unreachable from any root, which means no running code can ever access it again, so it is garbage and its memory can be reclaimed. Copying and compacting collectors do a variation where they relocate the live objects rather than freeing the dead ones in place, but the reachability determination is the same. A small banking example: a transfer object referenced by a local variable in an executing method is reachable through a stack root and kept; once that method returns and nothing else references the transfer, it becomes unreachable and is collected.

Now the circular-reference question, which is really a question about why Java does not use reference counting. A reference-counting scheme keeps, per object, a count of how many references point to it, and frees an object when its count hits zero. Reference counting has a famous flaw: two objects that reference each other each keep the other's count above zero, so even when nothing else refers to either of them, their counts never reach zero and they are never freed. That is a genuine leak in a pure reference-counting system. Java deliberately does not use reference counting; it uses reachability tracing from roots. Under tracing, the only question that matters is whether an object can be reached from a root, not how many references point at it. So if object A and object B reference each other but no root can reach either A or B, the tracing collector simply never marks them during the mark phase, and they are both swept as garbage. The mutual reference is irrelevant because it does not connect either object to any root.

The senior-level clarification I always add is the distinction between a reference cycle and an actual memory leak in Java. A cycle on its own is harmless and is collected normally. A real Java memory leak happens when an object remains reachable from a root even though the program will never use it again, for example an object still referenced by a static collection, a thread-local that is never cleared, or a listener that was registered and never deregistered. In those cases the object is not garbage by the collector's definition, because a live root really does reach it, so the collector correctly keeps it, and the fix is to break that root reference in the application code. This is also why heap-dump analysis asks "what retains this?" and follows the path to garbage-collection roots: finding the root reference that keeps an unused object alive is finding the leak. So the precise statement is that Java cannot leak merely from cycles, but it can leak from unintended reachability through a root.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India models a transaction and its reversal as two objects that reference each other, forming a cycle. A developer worried this cycle would leak memory. This is exactly the circular-reference question, and the answer is that once no root reaches either object, the tracing collector reclaims the whole cycle, so a cycle alone is never a leak.

Problem 2 — The same service really did leak, not from the cycle but because a static registry kept references to transactions forever. This is exactly the distinction between a harmless cycle and a true leak caused by unintended reachability from a root, and the fix was to stop the static root from retaining them.

In the mini-project we build a `Transaction` and a `Reversal` that reference each other (a cycle), drop all external references to them, and confirm via reachability reasoning and a weak-reference probe that the cycle is collected. We then show a static registry that genuinely retains objects, illustrating that the leak comes from the root, not the cycle.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/gcroots/GcRootsDemo.java

# Run it (verbose GC helps you see collections happen)
java -Xms128m -Xmx128m -Xlog:gc \
     -cp out com.bank.gcroots.GcRootsDemo

# To inspect roots in a heap dump: Eclipse MAT → right-click object →
# "Path to GC Roots" shows WHICH root (static field / thread / JNI) retains it.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transaction and a reversal that reference each other forming a cycle with no external root, and later one thousand transactions placed into a static registry.

Step 1: The helper method creates a Transaction and a Reversal and wires them to reference each other, forming a cycle. While the method runs, both are reachable through the method's local variables, which are stack roots.

Step 2: The method returns only a weak reference to the transaction. Weak references do not keep an object alive, so when the method returns and its locals disappear, no garbage-collection root reaches either object, even though they still reference each other.

Step 3: A collection is requested. The tracing collector starts from the roots and traverses the graph, but it never reaches the transaction or the reversal because no root leads to them; the mutual reference between them is irrelevant. Both are left unmarked and swept as garbage. The weak-reference probe returns null, confirming the cycle was collected, which proves a cycle alone is not a leak.

Step 4: The loop then places one thousand transactions into a static registry. The static field is a garbage-collection root, so every transaction it holds is reachable from a root and the collector correctly keeps all of them even after a collection. This is a genuine leak, caused not by any cycle but by unintended reachability from a root.

Step 5: Clearing the static registry breaks the root reference, after which the transactions become unreachable and eligible for collection, demonstrating that the fix for a real Java leak is to break the root reference in application code.

```text
[INFO] cycle (txn <-> reversal) collected after dropping roots? true  → circular refs are NOT a leak (reachability, not ref-counting)
[WARNING] static registry still retains 1000 transactions → reachable from a GC ROOT → genuine leak until cleared
[INFO] after clearing the static root, retained = 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  GC ROOTS: stack locals | static fields | JNI refs | threads | classloaders | monitors
     │ tracing starts HERE
     ▼
  mark everything reachable by following references

  CASE 1 — unreachable cycle (NOT a leak):
     (no root)
        Transaction ⇄ Reversal     ← reference each other
     neither reachable from a root → NOT marked → SWEPT (collected)
     → circular reference alone is NEVER a leak (tracing, not ref-count)

  CASE 2 — real leak (reachable from a root):
     static KEPT (GC ROOT) ──→ [ Transaction × 1000 ]
     reachable from root → MARKED → kept forever
     → leak = unintended reachability from a root
     fix: KEPT.clear()  (break the root reference)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — GC Roots, Tracing, Cycles ═══

  ┌─ GC Root categories ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ - stack: local vars & params of running threads        │
  │ - static fields of loaded classes                      │
  │ - JNI references (local + global) from native code     │
  │ - live Thread objects                                  │
  │ - class loaders + their loaded Class objects           │
  │ - monitors (objects being synchronized on)             │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Tracing (mark-sweep):
    MARK: from each root, traverse graph, mark reachable
    SWEEP: unmarked = unreachable = garbage → reclaim
    (copying/compacting = relocate live; same reachability rule)

  Why cycles are NOT a leak:
    ref-counting: A⇄B keep each other's count > 0 → never freed (leak)
    Java tracing: only reachability-from-root matters;
      A⇄B with NO root → unmarked → collected
    cycle ≠ leak.

  Real leak definition:
    object reachable from a root but never used again
    causes: static collection, ThreadLocal not removed,
            listener not deregistered, unbounded cache
    fix: break the ROOT reference (clear/deregister/bound)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Garbage-collection roots are the set of references that are inherently reachable, the starting points from which the collector begins tracing. The categories I name are: local variables and operand-stack entries in the frames of every running thread, because anything an executing method is using must be kept alive; static fields of loaded classes, because class statics live as long as the class is loaded; Java Native Interface references that native code holds, so objects handed to native code are not collected out from under it; live thread objects themselves; class loaders and the class objects they load; and objects currently being used as synchronization monitors. These are references that exist outside the ordinary object graph and are known to be live by definition.

A tracing collector then determines garbage by reachability in two conceptual phases. In the mark phase it starts from every root and traverses the object graph, following each reference transitively and marking every object it reaches as live. Because it follows references all the way through, it reaches the entire set of objects the program can still use. In the sweep phase, any object that was not marked is unreachable from every root, which means no running code can ever access it again, so it is garbage and its memory is reclaimed. Copying and compacting collectors relocate the live objects instead of freeing the dead ones in place, but the reachability determination is identical.

The circular-reference question is really about why Java does not use reference counting. A reference-counting scheme keeps a count per object of how many references point to it and frees it when the count hits zero, and its famous flaw is that two objects referencing each other each keep the other's count above zero, so even when nothing else refers to either of them, their counts never reach zero and they are never freed, which is a genuine leak. Java deliberately uses reachability tracing from roots instead, where the only thing that matters is whether an object can be reached from a root, not how many references point at it. So if object A and object B reference each other but no root can reach either one, the collector simply never marks them and sweeps both as garbage. The mutual reference is irrelevant because it does not connect either object to any root, which is exactly why a reference cycle is never a leak in Java.

The clarification I always finish with is the difference between a cycle and a real leak. A cycle on its own is harmless and collected normally. A true Java memory leak happens when an object stays reachable from a root even though the program will never use it again, for instance because it is still in a static collection, held by a thread-local that was never cleared, or referenced by a listener that was registered and never deregistered. In those cases a live root really does reach the object, so the collector correctly keeps it, and the fix is to break that root reference in the application code. This is also precisely why heap-dump analysis asks what retains an object and follows the path to garbage-collection roots: finding the root reference that keeps an unused object alive is finding the leak. So the precise statement I give is that Java cannot leak merely from reference cycles, but it absolutely can leak from unintended reachability through a root.

keyPoints: GC roots: starting points for reachability analysis
Types: thread stack local variables, static fields, JNI references, active monitors
Tracing: follow references from roots, mark everything reachable as live
Unreachable objects (including circular references) are garbage
Circular references are NOT a leak — if no root reaches them, they are collected
